cse-1995-a-1.approach: To clear chosen bits, AND with a mask that has 0s in those positions and 1s elsewhere; ANI does that with an immediate byte.

steps.title: Choose the mask
steps.body: Lower nibble must become 0, upper nibble must be kept: mask $= 1111\,0000_2 = \text{F0H}$.

steps.title: Choose the operation
steps.body: $x \land 0 = 0$ clears a bit, $x \land 1 = x$ keeps it. So `ANI F0H` gives $A \leftarrow A \land \text{F0H}$: lower four bits cleared, upper four unchanged.

optionAnalysis.reason: `XRI 0FH` complements (toggles) the lower four bits instead of clearing them.
AND with F0H forces bits 0–3 to 0 and keeps bits 4–7. Correct.
`XRI F0H` toggles the upper four bits and leaves the lower ones unchanged.
`ANI 0FH` clears the upper four bits and keeps the lower ones — the opposite.

cse-1995-a-1.shortcut: Clear → AND with 0s; set → OR with 1s; toggle → XOR with 1s.
pitfalls: Writing the mask for the bits you want to keep vs. clear the wrong way round (0FH vs F0H).
cse-1995-a-1.verification: Example: A = 3CH = 0011 1100; 3CH AND F0H = 30H = 0011 0000 — lower nibble cleared.

cse-1995-a-2.approach: Check each statement against the basic definitions of ROM, program counter, stack and flags.

steps.title: Test each claim
steps.body:
- ROM is read-only in normal operation.
- PC holds the address of the **next** instruction to fetch.
- A stack pushes and pops at the same end — Last In, First Out.
- Many instructions (data transfer such as MOV, LXI; jumps) leave the flags unchanged.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Only "Stack works on the principle of LIFO" is true.

answer.value: Stack works on the principle of LIFO

optionAnalysis.reason: ROM is Read-Only Memory; it is not written during normal operation.
PC points to the next instruction to be executed, not the last one executed.
Push and pop work at the top only, so the last item pushed is the first popped (LIFO). Correct.
Data-transfer and branch instructions (e.g. MOV, MVI, JMP in 8085) do not affect flags.

pitfalls: Confusing "PC = next instruction" with "PC = current/last instruction".
cse-1995-a-2.verification: In 8085, MOV A,B leaves all flags unchanged, so D is false; the other two are false by definition.

cse-1995-a-3.approach: Vectored means the device itself supplies the vector (address or number) that tells the CPU where its service routine is.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: In a **vectored** interrupt the interrupting device supplies an interrupt vector (an address, or an index into a vector table), so the CPU knows which service routine to run without polling.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: A branch to one fixed memory location for every source is a **non-vectored** interrupt — the CPU then has to poll to find the source.

answer.value: The interrupting source supplies the branch information through an interrupt vector

optionAnalysis.reason: A single fixed branch location describes a non-vectored interrupt.
The source supplies the vector that gives the branch target. Correct.
The branch address does not come from a CPU register; it comes from the device or a vector table indexed by the device.
B is correct, so "None of the above" is wrong.

pitfalls: 8085 RST 5.5/6.5/7.5 branch to fixed addresses but each line has its own address — still not option A's "single fixed location for all".
cse-1995-a-3.verification: 8086 INTR: the device puts a type number on the bus during INTA, and the CPU reads the vector table at type × 4 — the source supplies the branch information.

cse-1995-a-4.approach: Resolve the dangling else: the else belongs to the nearest unmatched if (the inner one). Then the outer test is false, so nothing runs.

steps.title: Parse
steps.body:
The else binds to the inner `if`:
```pascal
if X > Y then
   begin
     if X < 0 then X := abs(X) else X := 2*X
   end;
```

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.body: $X = -10,\ Y = 20$: $X > Y$ is $-10 > 20$ = false. The whole inner `if–else` is skipped, so $X$ stays $-10$.

optionAnalysis.reason: 10 = abs(X) would need both $X > Y$ and $X < 0$; $X > Y$ is false.
−20 = 2·X would only happen if the else were attached to the outer `if` (wrong binding).
Outer condition false and the else belongs to the inner if, so X is unchanged at −10. Correct.
C is correct.

pitfalls: Matching the else with the outer if — that gives −20 (option B).
cse-1995-a-4.verification: Same rule as C/Java: an else always pairs with the closest preceding unmatched if.

cse-1995-a-5.approach: Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts each recursively and merges — the textbook divide-and-conquer pattern.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Divide: split into two halves. Conquer: sort each half recursively. Combine: merge the two sorted halves in $O(n)$.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n\log n)$ — a divide-and-conquer recurrence.

optionAnalysis.reason: Split, solve sub-problems, merge — divide and conquer. Correct.
Backtracking explores and undoes choices (e.g. N-queens); merge sort never backtracks.
Heuristic search (e.g. A*) uses estimates to guide search; sorting is deterministic.
Greedy algorithms make one locally best choice per step (e.g. Kruskal); merge sort does not.

cse-1995-a-5.verification: Quick sort and binary search follow the same divide-and-conquer pattern.

cse-1995-a-6.approach: Locality means a program reuses recently used data (temporal) and nearby addresses (spatial); a small fast cache holding those blocks exploits this.

steps.title: Locality
steps.body: Temporal: a word used now is likely used again soon. Spatial: words near it are likely used soon.

steps.title: Who exploits it
steps.body: A cache keeps recently used blocks (temporal) and loads whole blocks (spatial), so most accesses hit in fast memory. Without locality a cache would give no benefit.

optionAnalysis.reason: Interrupts are about asynchronous event handling, not memory access patterns.
DMA transfers I/O data without the CPU; it is not justified by locality.
Polling is a way of checking device status.
Caches work because of temporal and spatial locality. Correct.

cse-1995-a-6.verification: Virtual memory/paging is the other mechanism that relies on locality; none of the other options do.

cse-1995-a-7.approach: In paged segmentation each segment is paged; if the segment table itself is larger than one page it too must be paged, which needs a page table for it.

steps.title: Why page any table
steps.body: A table must sit in memory. If it is larger than one page/frame, it cannot be placed contiguously in a single frame, so it is split over pages — and then a page table is needed to find those pages.

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: So the segment table needs its own page table exactly when it is too large to fit in one page (as in MULTICS, where segment tables can be huge).

answer.value: The segment table is often too large to fit in one page

optionAnalysis.reason: A large segment table spills over several pages, so it must itself be paged. Correct.
Segments spread over pages explains why each **segment** needs a page table, not the segment table.
True of paged segmentation in general, but it does not explain why the segment table itself is paged.
Where the base register points is a consequence of paging the segment table, not the reason for it.

pitfalls: Choosing B: that is the reason segments have page tables, not the reason the segment table does.
cse-1995-a-7.verification: Same reasoning as multilevel paging: a page table bigger than one page is itself paged.

cse-1995-a-8.approach: Belady's anomaly (more frames causing more faults) only happens in algorithms that are not stack algorithms; FIFO is the classic example.

steps.title: Stack property
steps.body: For OPT and LRU, the pages in memory with $k$ frames are always a subset of those with $k+1$ frames, so adding frames can never add faults.

steps.title: FIFO counter-example
steps.body: Reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: FIFO gives **9** faults with 3 frames but **10** faults with 4 frames.

optionAnalysis.reason: Optimal is a stack algorithm; it never shows the anomaly.
LRU is a stack algorithm; it never shows the anomaly.
FIFO is not a stack algorithm and has the known 9 → 10 fault example. Correct.
Includes Optimal, which does not show the anomaly.

cse-1995-a-8.verification: Count FIFO on 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: 9 faults with 3 frames, 10 with 4.

cse-1995-a-9.approach: Write the definition directly: one letter, followed by zero or more symbols each of which is a letter or a digit.

steps.title: Translate
steps.body: "a letter" $\to L$; "followed by any number of letters or digits" $\to (L \cup D)^*$. Concatenate: $L.(L \cup D)^*$.

steps.title: Check the others
steps.body: Each wrong option either allows a leading digit or forces letters and digits to alternate.

optionAnalysis.reason: $(L\cup D)^+$ accepts strings starting with a digit, e.g. "9a".
First symbol a letter, then any mix of letters and digits. Correct.
$(L.D)^*$ accepts the empty string and forces letter-digit pairs, so it rejects "ab".
$L.(L.D)^*$ forces strict alternation after the first letter, so it rejects "ab" and "a12".

cse-1995-a-9.verification: Test "x", "ab", "a1b2c": only B accepts all three and rejects "1a".

cse-1995-a-10.approach: Classify by the most general rule form. A rule with more than one symbol on the left rules out context-free; then check whether every rule is non-contracting.
cse-1995-a-10.given:
| Rule | LHS length | RHS length |
|---|---|---|
| $S \to a\alpha b \mid b\alpha c \mid aB$ | 1 | 3, 3, 2 |
| $S \to aS \mid b$ | 1 | 2, 1 |
| $S \to \alpha bb \mid ab$ | 1 | 3, 2 |
| $b\alpha \to bdb \mid b$ | 2 | 3, 1 |

steps.title: Not context-free
steps.body: The rule $b\alpha \to bdb$ has two symbols on the left: $\alpha$ is rewritten only when it follows $b$. So the grammar is not context-free, hence also not regular and not LR(k) (LR(k) grammars are context-free).

steps.title: Context-sensitive
steps.body: Rules of the form $b\alpha \to bdb$ rewrite $\alpha$ in the context $b\_\,$, which is the context-sensitive form. Among the options the intended answer is **context sensitive**.

steps.title: Caveat
steps.body: $b\alpha \to b$ shrinks the string ($|b\alpha| = 2 > |b| = 1$). Strictly, a contracting rule makes the grammar unrestricted (type 0). No such option exists, so the accepted answer is context sensitive.

optionAnalysis.reason: A context-free grammar has a single non-terminal on the left; $b\alpha \to \dots$ has two symbols.
Regular grammars are a subset of CFGs, so it cannot be regular either.
The rewriting of $\alpha$ depends on the context $b$ — context-sensitive form. Accepted answer.
LR(k) grammars are context-free, which this grammar is not.

pitfalls: Looking only at the $S$-rules (all CFG-like) and missing the $b\alpha$ rule.
cse-1995-a-10.verification: Each of A, B, D requires a single non-terminal on every LHS, so all three fail on the $b\alpha$ rules. C is the only option left and matches the stored key; the type-0 caveat is in the review note.

cse-1995-a-11.approach: Names in a macro (or procedure) definition header are placeholders; the values substituted at each call are the actual parameters.

steps.title: Definition vs call
steps.body: In `macro Add x,y`, the names `x` and `y` appear in the **definition** and stand for whatever is passed in.

steps.title: Expansion
steps.body: A call such as `Add A,B` substitutes the actual parameters `A`, `B` for `x`, `y` in the body (`Load B / Mul A / Store B`). So `x`, `y` are formal parameters.

optionAnalysis.reason: They are not storage locations; they are replaced textually during expansion.
Too general — every name is an identifier; it does not describe their role.
Actual parameters are the arguments supplied at the call/expansion, not the names in the definition.
Placeholders in the definition header are formal parameters. Correct.

cse-1995-a-11.verification: Same terminology as procedures: parameters in the declaration are formal, arguments at the call are actual.

cse-1995-a-12.approach: The distance of a code is the minimum Hamming distance over all pairs of distinct codewords; one pair at distance 2 already fixes it once no pair is at distance 1.

steps.title: Distances from 000000
steps.body: Equal to the weights: 3, 3, 3, 3, 6.

cse-1995-a-13.approach: A string is a complete token without lookahead only if no longer token can start with it. Keywords can be prefixes of identifiers; "<>" cannot be extended.

steps.title: Keywords
steps.body: `begin` could be the start of an identifier such as `beginner`; `program` could start `programs`. The lexer must read the next character to know whether the keyword has ended.

steps.title: The <> operator
steps.body: In Pascal no token is longer than `<>` and begins with `<>`, so once `<>` is read it is definitely the not-equal token.

`program` may be a prefix of an identifier (e.g. `programX`), so lookahead is needed.

I and II need lookahead.

cse-1995-a-14.approach: Separately compiled modules are relocated by the linker, so final absolute addresses of internal symbols are not known at compile time and are not stored.

steps.title: What a linker needs
steps.body: The object code itself, relocation information (which address fields to adjust), and the symbol table of externally visible definitions and external references, so modules can be joined.

steps.title: What it does not need
steps.body: Internal symbols are addressed relative to the module start; absolute addresses are only fixed after the linker/loader places the module, so they are not part of the object module.

optionAnalysis.reason: The object code is the main content of the module.
Relocation bits tell the linker which fields to adjust when the module is moved.
Defined external (public) symbols are needed to resolve references from other modules.
Absolute addresses are not known before linking; internal symbols need only relative addresses. Correct.

cse-1995-a-14.verification: In ELF/COFF files a .o has .text, relocation entries and a symbol table, but all addresses are section-relative.

cse-1995-a-15.approach: Time sharing needs every user to get a response quickly, which round robin gives by handing each process a fixed time quantum in turn.

steps.title: Requirement
steps.body: Interactive users share the CPU; each must get the CPU regularly so that response time is bounded.

steps.title: Round robin
steps.body: With $n$ ready processes and quantum $q$, each waits at most $(n-1)q$ before running again — preemptive and fair, exactly what time sharing needs.

optionAnalysis.reason: SJF needs burst lengths in advance and can starve long jobs.
Round robin preempts after a time quantum, giving every user regular turns. Correct.
FCFS is non-preemptive; one long job blocks everyone (convoy effect).
Elevator (SCAN) is a disk-scheduling algorithm, not CPU scheduling.

cse-1995-a-15.verification: Classic time-sharing systems (e.g. CTSS, UNIX) are built on quantum-based round robin variants.

cse-1995-a-16.approach: In the standard merge, each comparison outputs one element, so at most m + n − 1 comparisons are made.

steps.title: Count comparisons
steps.body: Each comparison places one element into the output. When one list empties, the rest of the other is copied with no comparisons. So at most $m + n - 1$ comparisons.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: Worst case, e.g. when the lists interleave: $m+n-1 = \Theta(m+n)$, so $O(m+n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $O(m)$ ignores the $n$ elements; it fails when $n \gg m$ with interleaving values.
$O(n)$ ignores the $m$ elements, for the same reason.
At most $m+n-1$ comparisons. Correct.
Logarithmic comparisons cannot place $m+n$ elements in order.

cse-1995-a-16.verification: m = n = 2: [1,3] and [2,4] need 3 = m + n − 1 comparisons.

cse-1995-a-17.approach: Count edges two ways: each node except the root has one parent edge, and each node contributes edges equal to its number of children.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Let $n_0, n_1, n_2$ = number of nodes with 0, 1, 2 children. Total nodes $N = n_0 + n_1 + n_2$; edges $E = N - 1$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body: With $n_0 = n$ leaves: $n_2 = n - 1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\log_2 n$ is roughly the height of a balanced tree with $n$ leaves, not the count of degree-2 nodes.
Edge counting gives $n_2 = n_0 - 1 = n - 1$. Correct.
$n$ is one too many (off by one).
$2^n$ is far too large; a tree with $n$ leaves has fewer than $2n$ nodes.

cse-1995-a-18.approach: Count three-digit numbers with no 7 digit by digit and divide by the 900 three-digit numbers.

steps.title: Favourable
steps.body: Hundreds digit: 1–9 without 7 → 8 choices. Tens and units: 0–9 without 7 → 9 choices each. Count $= 8 \times 9 \times 9 = 648$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $(9/10)^3 = 0.729$ treats the hundreds digit as having 10 choices, including 0.
$27/75 = 0.36$ does not match.

cse-1995-a-19.approach: A symmetric and transitive relation is reflexive only on elements that are related to something; an isolated element breaks reflexivity, while the full relation is reflexive — so neither A, B nor C always holds.

steps.title: Not necessarily reflexive
steps.body: $A = \{1,2\}$, $R = \{(1,1)\}$: symmetric and transitive, but $(2,2) \notin R$, so not reflexive. So A and B are false.

steps.title: Not necessarily non-reflexive
steps.body: $R = A \times A$ is symmetric, transitive **and** reflexive (an equivalence relation). So C ("R is not reflexive") is also false in general.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: None of A, B, C holds for every such $R$ → D.

optionAnalysis.reason: $R = \{(1,1)\}$ on $\{1,2\}$ is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive.
Same counter-example; also a partial order needs antisymmetry, which is not given.
$R = A \times A$ is symmetric, transitive and reflexive, so "not reflexive" fails.
No one of the statements is always true. Correct.

pitfalls: The "proof" $aRb \wedge bRa \Rightarrow aRa$ needs some $b$ with $aRb$; it fails for isolated elements.
cse-1995-a-19.verification: Both counter-examples checked against the definitions.

steps.title: Elements of S
steps.body: $S = \{\{\phi\},\ 1,\ \{2,3\}\}$ has three elements: the set $\{\phi\}$, the number 1, and the set $\{2,3\}$. So $|S| = 3$.

steps.title: Power set
steps.body: Each element is either in or out of a subset, so $|P(S)| = 2^{|S|} = 2^3 = 8$.

4 would mean $|S| = 2$.
$2^3 = 8$. Correct.

cse-1995-a-21.approach: Let $f(x) = x - \cos x$. It changes sign on $[0,\pi]$ and is increasing, so it has exactly one root.

steps.title: Sign change
steps.body: $f(0) = 0 - 1 = -1 < 0$; $f(\pi) = \pi - (-1) = \pi + 1 > 0$. By the IVT there is at least one root.

steps.title: Monotonic
steps.body: $f'(x) = 1 + \sin x \ge 0$ on $[0,\pi]$ (it equals 1 at the ends and is > 1 inside). So $f$ is strictly increasing and has at most one root.

optionAnalysis.reason: IVT gives at least one root since $f$ goes from $-1$ to $\pi+1$.
At least one (IVT) and at most one (strictly increasing). Correct.
A strictly increasing function cannot have two roots.
Same reason — at most one root.

cse-1995-a-22.approach: Write the slope condition as a differential equation, separate variables and integrate.

steps.title: Equation
steps.body: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2x}{y} \Rightarrow y\,dy = -2x\,dx$.

steps.title: Integrate
steps.body: $\dfrac{y^2}{2} = -x^2 + c \Rightarrow 2x^2 + y^2 = 2c = C$.

steps.title: Identify
steps.body: $2x^2 + y^2 = C$ ($C > 0$) has unequal positive coefficients on $x^2$ and $y^2$: an ellipse, $\dfrac{x^2}{C/2} + \dfrac{y^2}{C} = 1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: A straight line has constant slope; here the slope varies with $x$ and $y$.
A parabola has only one squared term; here both $x^2$ and $y^2$ appear.
A circle needs equal coefficients; here they are 2 and 1. (Slope $-x/y$ would give a circle.)
$2x^2 + y^2 = C$ is an ellipse. Correct.

cse-1995-a-23.approach: $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 = 0$ is a pair of real lines through the origin iff $h^2 \ge ab$. Find which k breaks this.

steps.title: Match coefficients
steps.body: $a = 4$, $2h = -8 \Rightarrow h = -4$, $b = k$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: Real lines need $h^2 \ge ab$: $16 \ge 4k \Rightarrow k \le 4$.

steps.title: Check options
steps.body: $k = 0, 2, 3$ satisfy $k \le 4$; $k = 9$ gives $16 - 36 = -20 < 0$, so only the origin satisfies the equation — no real lines.

optionAnalysis.reason: $k = 0$: $4x(x - 2y) = 0$, the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 2y$.
$k = 2$: $h^2 - ab = 16 - 8 = 8 > 0$, two real lines.
$k = 9$: $16 - 36 < 0$, no real lines. Correct.
